title: Junk News and Bots during the German Parliamentary Election: What are German Voters Sharing over Twitter? (COMPROP Data Memo 2017.7)
screen_reason: Observational analysis of URLs shared in election-hashtag tweets: 11,646 shared URLs classified by source type, with 1,055 classified as junk news and a stated 11.5% of 'relevant' political content being junk news. A share of shared links carrying junk news from platform data = SHARING (content_share).

estimates.measure_type: % of relevant political news and information links shared in German election-hashtag tweets that came from junk news sources
estimates.value_raw: 11.5 (percent of relevant content that is "Junk News"); Junk News N=1,055 of Relevant Content Subtotal 9,182
estimates.denominator: 9,182 'relevant' political news and information URLs shared by Twitter users tweeting German election hashtags (the 11,646 classified URLs minus social-media-platform links, other non-political content and inaccessible links)
estimates.definition: A shared URL counted in the numerator if its source was classified 'Junk News' in the grounded typology: propaganda and ideologically extreme, hyperpartisan or conspiratorial political news and information, much of it deliberately produced false reporting, produced by organizations that do not employ professional journalists and using attention-grabbing techniques.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Junk news websites deliberately publish misleading, deceptive or incorrect information purporting to be real news about politics, economics or culture."
estimates.n: 9,182 URLs (relevant political news and information links)
estimates.source_quote: Germany II. Sample, before voting. Parliamentary 51.0 13.4 7.4 11.5 1.4 1.4:1 4.4:1 Election. 1-10 September 2017, 985K tweets.
estimates.page_loc: Table 4 (p. 6), row 'Germany II'; Table 3 (p. 5); Findings and Analysis, fourth paragraph (p. 4)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Source-level classification against a dictionary of classified news and political-information sources carried over from the authors' earlier German Federal Presidency memo, which automatically classified 88.9% of URLs; a random 10% sample of the remaining URLs was hand-coded by three coders fluent in German and familiar with the media landscape, trained together over two days and required to pass a test of ground-truth URLs. No intercoder reliability statistic (kappa or otherwise) is reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Our dataset contains approximately 984,713 tweets generated by 149,573 unique users that were collected between the 1st and the 10th of September 2017, using hashtags associated with the primary political parties in Germany, the major candidates, and the election itself. ... From our dataset of 984,713 tweets, we selected all of the tweets that contained URLs. Between 1-10 September, Twitter users in Germany shared 115,563 links on the platform. URLs that pointed towards another tweet were removed from our sample ... If Twitter users shared more than one URL in their tweet, only the first URL was analyzed. This approach yielded in 11,646 URLs that were then analyzed.
estimates.notes: 1,055/9,182 = 11.49%, matching the verbatim 11.5 in Table 4. Table 4's column headers are rotated in the PDF text layer; the mapping is fixed by the running text, which states 51.0% professional news, 7.4% automated content and a 4.4:1 professional-to-junk ratio for Germany II, leaving 11.5 as the junk-news column and 1.4 as the Russian-sources column. Junk news is defined at SOURCE level (a list of outlets), so breadth is left blank per schema. This is a non-peer-reviewed COMPROP data memo.

estimates.measure_type: % of ALL classified URLs shared in German election-hashtag tweets that came from junk news sources (wider denominator, including non-political, social-media and inaccessible links)
estimates.denominator: 11,646 URLs shared in tweets carrying German election hashtags and classified by the team (first URL per tweet, tweet-to-tweet links removed)
estimates.definition: Same numerator as the primary row (source classified 'Junk News'), but expressed over every classified URL rather than only the 'relevant' political subset.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Junk news websites deliberately publish misleading, deceptive or incorrect information purporting to be real news about politics, economics or culture."

estimates.notes: DERIVED, NOT STATED: the authors never print 9.1%; it is the exact part/whole share of two verbatim Table 3 counts with the same denominator (1,055 junk news URLs / 11,646 total classified URLs = 9.06%), which R8 permits. Kept because the difference between this and the headline 11.5% is purely a denominator choice (relevant political content vs all shared links) - exactly the methodological divergence the review codes. An adjudicator who prefers only author-stated values should drop this row and keep the first.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) 'The ratio of links to professionally produced news to junk news was 4.4:1' (and 'roughly four to one') - a ratio, not a share with a denominator; (2) junk news as 32.2% of the 3,277 'Other Political News and Information' links (Table 3) - a share within a heterogeneous residual category (junk + other political + citizen/civil society + humour + Russia + religion), which is neither a prevalence nor a within-misinformation falsity share; (3) 40.2% professional news, 10.5% professional political, 17.8% other, 3.6% inaccessible (Table 3), and 51.0% professional news / 13.4% parties-government-experts / 1.4% Russian sources (Table 4) - non-misinformation categories; (4) automation figures (7.4% of traffic from highly automated accounts; 15.0% for AfD hashtags; 92 high-frequency accounts; Table 2) - bot activity, not misinformation content; (5) party traffic shares (AfD 30.1%, CDU/CSU 18.2%, etc., Table 1) - attention, not falsity; (6) every other row of Table 4 (USA-Michigan 33.8% junk, France I 7.2%, France II 16.4%, UK I 12.6%, UK II 16.5%, Germany I 12.5%) - these are figures this memo carries over from the authors' own EARLIER memos on other elections, i.e. values cited from elsewhere, which R8 excludes; the Germany I (February 2017 Federal Presidency) junk-news figure of 12.5% belongs to reference 6, not to this study. Methodological caveat for the adjudicator: only 88.9% of URLs were classifiable from the existing source dictionary and the remainder was handled by coding 'a random sample of 10 percent of the rest', yet Table 3 totals to all 11,646 URLs; how the 10% sample was projected onto the full set is not explained, so the junk-news count carries unstated extrapolation.

rob.design: Non-peer-reviewed COMPROP data memo. Sampling frame: Twitter Streaming API (at most a 1% sample of global public tweets) filtered on hashtags for the major German parties, candidates and the election, 1-10 September 2017; 984,713 tweets from 149,573 unique users; 115,563 links shared, reduced to 11,646 analysed URLs after dropping tweet-to-tweet URLs and keeping only the first URL per tweet. Classification procedure: an existing dictionary of classified sources auto-classified 88.9% of URLs; a random 10% sample of the rest was coded by three German-fluent coders familiar with the media landscape, trained together over two days and required to pass a ground-truth URL test. Reliability as reported: NONE (no kappa, no double-coding statistic). Authors acknowledge the hashtag frame may miss minor hashtags and may capture off-topic tweets.
rob.item6_quote: Junk News. This content includes various forms of propaganda and ideologically extreme, hyper-partisan, or conspiratorial political news and information. Much of this content is deliberately produced false reporting. It seeks to persuade readers about the moral virtues or failings of organizations, causes or people and presents commentary as a news product. This content is produced by organizations that do not employ professional journalists, and the content uses attention grabbing techniques, lots of pictures, moving images, excessive capitalization, ad hominem attacks, emotionally charged words and pictures, unsafe generalizations and other logical fallacies.
rob.item10_quote: Of the tweets sharing URLs captured in this sample, some 11,646 tweets included links to political news and information. ... Junk News 1,055 ...
